## Direct-Use Rules

- BASIC ROM must be banked in (`$0001` LORAM+HIRAM set). KERNAL ROM must also be visible for I/O and error reporting.
- Many failures jump to `$A437` (`ERROR`) rather than returning a status code.
- Prefer KERNAL APIs for files/devices and dynamic keyboard or tokenized program install for statements.
- Best reusable BASIC targets: `FRMEVL`, `FRMNUM`, `GETBYT`, `GETADR`, `PTRGET`, `FOUT`, `MOVFM`, `MOVMF`, `LNKPRG`, `CLR`.
- Avoid direct statement entries unless a wrapper controls `TXTPTR`, stack, BASIC vectors, error recovery, and runtime pointers.

# Commodore Disk Drives — 1541, 1571, 1581

**Scope:** Commodore floppy drives used with the C64/C128 via the IEC serial bus.  
Each drive contains an internal 6502 CPU and DOS ROM implementing a self‑contained filesystem.  
Main reference drive: **1541 (DOS 2.6)**; extensions for **1571 (DOS 3.0)** and **1581 (DOS 10.0)** below.

## 1571 — Double‑Sided Drive (DOS 3.0)

**Medium:** 5¼″ double‑sided DD, 70 tracks (35 × 2).  
**Capacity:** ~349 KB (1368 blocks). **DOS:** 3.0.  
Reads/writes 1541 disks (side A only); auto‑flips heads; supports burst mode with C128.

# C64 Game Architecture: Frame Loop, Budgets, Memory Maps

**Summary:** A C64 game is a frame-synchronous state machine: a raster IRQ chain does the timing-critical display and sound work, the main loop does one frame of logic per frame and hands results over through a flag. Decide the memory map and the frame budget before writing code. Templates below cover a stock 64 KB game, a small single-screen game and an Ultimate game streaming from REU.
**Read when:** starting any game, before choosing addresses, VIC bank, loader or IRQ layout. Techniques (code) are in `c64://gamedev/techniques`.

Marks: "(unverified)" = not confirmed against a primary source. Targets: MODERN = Ultimate devices, AUTHENTIC = stock C64 (see `c64://gamedev/index`).

records.name: data/gamedev/architecture.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/gamedev/architecture.md#2. State machine -->
## 2. State machine
- One byte `state`, jump table of `init/update/exit` per state: BOOT, TITLE (attract), MENU, PLAY, PAUSE, GAMEOVER, HISCORE.
- State change = set `next_state`; apply at frame start (never mid-frame): run `exit`, reset VIC/IRQ list for the new state, run `init`.
- Each state owns its screen layout and IRQ list; shared modules: input, sound, sprites, RNG, score/BCD.
- Keep entities in structure-of-arrays tables (`x_lo,x_hi,y,type,frame,state`), at most 256 entries each, so access is `lda tab,x`.
- Fixed-point positions (8.8) with velocities; screen position = high byte; do collisions on high bytes.

records.name: data/gamedev/architecture.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/gamedev/architecture.md#3. Frame budget -->
## 3. Frame budget
| | PAL (6569) | NTSC (6567R8) |
|---|---|---|
| CPU clock | 985,248 Hz | 1,022,727 Hz |
| Cycles per line x lines | 63 x 312 | 65 x 263 |
| Cycles per frame | 19,656 | 17,095 |
| Frame rate | 50.125 Hz | 59.826 Hz |
| Visible text rows | 25 badlines in lines `$30`-`$F7` | same |
- Older NTSC 6567R56A: 64 x 262 = 16,768 cycles (rare). Detect machine type at runtime (see techniques).
- Badline: the VIC takes about 43 cycles, the CPU keeps about 20 of 63. 25 badlines cost 1,081 cycles per PAL frame (measured 2026-11-13 on an Ultimate 64 Elite and a C64U at 1 MHz, matches VICE). Eight double-height sprites cost a further 802 cycles per frame (about 19 per line over 42 lines). Border/vblank lines are fully free (about 112 lines PAL).
- Practical free time for a 1 MHz game: PAL about 17,800 cycles with a full text screen and 8 double-height sprites (measured); NTSC about 15,000. Budget the slower NTSC and let PAL idle, or scale by frame count.
- Typical per-frame costs (estimates, unverified): music player 500-1,500; 8-sprite update 800; software scroll column copy 1,500-3,000; 24-sprite multiplexer sort 1,000-2,500.
- Measure instead of guessing: set `$D020` to a colour when entering a routine, restore when leaving; the border band height is its cost in raster lines (1 line = 63 cycles PAL). Do this in VICE and capture the frame (`c64_graphics` `capture_frame`).

### B. Small single-screen game (AUTHENTIC, easiest), VIC bank 0, KERNAL on
`$0801` stub; code at `$0810`-`$0FFF`; music at `$1000` (typical PSID load address; `$1000-$1FFF` is not visible as RAM to the VIC, so no graphics there); screen `$0400`; sprite shapes at `$2000-$27FF`; charset `$2800` or `$3800`; extra code/data `$4000+`. Use the KERNAL IRQ at `$0314` and chain to `$EA31` for keyboard, or `$EA81` to skip it.

### D. Disk-based RPG / adventure (AUTHENTIC)
Resident engine `$0900-$4FFF`, text/data banks loaded into a fixed window (for example `$5000-$9FFF`) on demand from disk (fastloader recommended, see toolchain); keep save game as one small file; keep a RAM copy of the directory map. On MODERN replace disk streaming by REU fetches.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/gamedev/architecture.md#6. Architecture checklist -->
## 6. Architecture checklist
1. Target chosen and stated; features detected with fallback message (MODERN) or absent (AUTHENTIC).
2. Memory map written first, all addresses in one include file, build asserts on overlaps.
3. VIC bank, `$01` play state, vector setup decided; NMI neutralised.
4. IRQ list designed: lines, order, who acknowledges `$D019`, music line, no two entries closer than the worst-case handler time.
5. Frame budget measured on NTSC timing (authentic) or by frame-count independence (modern).
6. Double-buffered hand-over between main loop and IRQ.
7. State machine with init/update/exit per state; hi-score and settings persistence (disk file or UCI file write) designed up front.
8. Loader/packer plan (single PRG, multipart, cartridge, REU preload); a golden checksum per release build.
9. Both PAL and NTSC tested (VICE: set machine model), music speed and gameplay tempo corrected.
10. Test tiers: logic in VICE, then hardware gate; capture a frame per milestone.

<!-- Source: data/gamedev/references.md#What modern Ultimate games do differently -->
### What modern Ultimate games do differently
- World in REU, fetched on demand (Doom C64U, ReadyOS); load by UCI or preload, not by disk.
- Turbo is detected, measured against the raster counter, and tolerates 48 MHz machines and the about 2 s forced 1 MHz window after reset.
- Turbo headroom buys software rendering and rich music engines (Doom, Heartbeat), not hardware tricks.
- Upic (border-colour per-pixel) suits stills and adventure graphics, not scrolling action; needs PAL, turbo registers, palette UCI (firmware 3.15 or later; older C64U firmware lacks it, unverified).
- PCM from REU through Ultimate Audio next to several SIDs.
- UCI for files and TCP; never wait on it inside a frame (palette writes measured at tens of ms).
- Program ships a `.cfg` that sets turbo and REU, listing both Turbo Control value names; normal edition plus Elite edition as fallback.
- Timing verified on hardware (frame hash, positive controls, tests at 1/16/64 MHz); VICE only for function.

records.name: data/gamedev/techniques.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/gamedev/techniques.md#1. Raster IRQ and IRQ chains -->
- Decimal flag is not cleared on interrupt on the NMOS 6510: use `cld` in any handler that touches arithmetic.
- Latency: IRQ entry takes 7 cycles plus the instruction in progress (0-7 more), so the first line of a handler jitters by up to 7 cycles. Bad lines add up to 40 cycles of CPU stall (see architecture).
- Stable raster (needed for cycle-exact colour bars, border opening, hi-res tricks): the double-IRQ method. IRQ 1 fires on line N, installs IRQ 2 for line N+1, saves SP (`tsx`), enables interrupts (`cli`) and runs a NOP sled; IRQ 2 fires during a NOP, so jitter drops to 0-1 cycles; it restores SP (`txs`), burns cycles to the end of the line, and compares `$D012` twice to remove the last cycle (`lda $d012; cmp $d012; beq +`). Exact cycle counts depend on sprites and bad lines on that line; tune with a border-colour change and capture (`capture_frame`). Sketch only (unverified).
- MODERN: raster-exact code tuned for 1 MHz cycle counts is not cycle-exact in real time under turbo; keep cycle-critical effects at 1 MHz or measure on hardware. Prefer effects that need only line accuracy (scroll split, charset switch, colour changes).
- Sprites reused below another sprite, status-bar splits, `$D018`/`$D016` switches all hang on this chain.
**Seen in:** Oscar64 `rasterirq.h` library (IRQ chain with register-write lists), Tony (raster "copper" list), Cadaver multiplexer (hand-rolled precomputed chain).

## 4. Collision
| Method | Use | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| `$D01E` sprite-sprite, `$D01F` sprite-background | cheap coarse test, 8 hardware sprites | bits are latched, cleared on read: read once per frame and keep the copy; bit = hardware sprite, not virtual; after multiplexing a bit may belong to either user; in multicolour char/sprite data only bit pairs `%10`/`%11` count as foreground for background collision (standard); pixel-exact, so small hitboxes need software |
| Software bounding box | player vs enemies, bullets | compare high bytes or use tables |
| Tile lookup | player vs walls/platforms | cell = ((x-24)>>3, (y-50)>>3) for sprite coordinates on a 40x25 screen; read the map/screen byte, look up a flag table (solid, ladder, deadly) |
- 8-bit overlap trick: a 256-byte table `ok[d]` indexed by `(x1-x2)` (unsigned wrap) returns 1 when |dx| < width; page-aligned. Test dx then dy.
- Sprite coordinates: X 24-343 is the 320-pixel text area, Y 50-249 the 200 lines; X needs the MSB in `$D010`.
- Check collisions in the main loop after movement, not in the IRQ; use the hardware flags only to prefilter.
**Seen in:** Oscar64 `hscrollshmup` (page-aligned overlap table), Tetris C64 (tile checks only).

| c64bridge `upload_run_asm` | asm (basic subset) | zero setup, good for snippets and tests; no macros/segments | built in |
Rule of thumb: IRQ chains, multiplexer, scroll copy and music glue in assembly; game logic, data tables and tools in assembly or Oscar64. Pin tool versions; check KickAssembler redistribution terms before bundling.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite and Charset Workflows Best Practices -->
# Sprite and Charset Workflows Best Practices

This guide provides proven workflows and best practices for creating, managing, and deploying sprites and custom character sets on the Commodore 64.

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Workflow Overview -->
## Sprite Workflow Overview

Sprites are hardware-accelerated movable graphics objects. Each sprite is 24×21 pixels with support for multicolour or hires modes.

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Basic Sprite Workflow -->
### Basic Sprite Workflow

1. **Design**: Create 24×21 pixel bitmap (monochrome or multicolour)
2. **Encode**: Convert to 63-byte sprite data format
3. **Upload**: Place sprite data in memory ($0340-$07FF recommended for safety)
4. **Configure**: Set sprite pointer, position, colour, and enable flags
5. **Verify**: Read screen or sprite registers to confirm appearance

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Memory Layout -->
### Sprite Memory Layout

Each sprite requires 63 bytes (24×21 pixels / 8 bits per byte):

- 21 rows of 3 bytes each
- Bit 1 = pixel on, Bit 0 = pixel off (hires mode)
- In multicolour mode, 2 bits per pixel define 4 colours

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Safe Sprite Data Locations -->
### Safe Sprite Data Locations

Use these memory ranges to avoid conflicts:

- `$0340-$03FF` - Cassette buffer (192 bytes, safe when not using tape)
- `$C000-$CFFF` - RAM under BASIC ROM (4KB, requires bank switching)
- `$2000-$3FFF` - Screen/bitmap alternatives (8KB when not displaying there)

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Colour Selection -->
### Sprite Colour Selection

- Individual sprite colour: `$D027-$D02E` (one per sprite)
- Multicolour shared colours: `$D025` (shared 1), `$D026` (shared 2)
- Background colour: `$D021`

Choose high-contrast colours for visibility:

- White (1) on black (0) background
- Yellow (7) or cyan (3) for highlights
- Avoid grey on grey or similar-hue combinations

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Basic Charset Workflow -->
### Basic Charset Workflow

1. **Design**: Create 8×8 pixel bitmaps for each character
2. **Encode**: Convert to 8-byte character definitions
3. **Upload**: Place charset in 2KB memory block ($2000, $2800, $3000, or $3800)
4. **Configure**: Point VIC-II to custom charset via `$D018`
5. **Test**: POKE characters to screen and verify appearance

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Switching Charsets -->
### Switching Charsets

Configure VIC-II register `$D018`:

- Bits 1-3 control charset pointer
- Formula: (charset_address / 2048) << 1
- Example: For charset at $2000, POKE 53272, (53272 AND 240) OR ((8192/2048) << 1)

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Multiplexing -->
### Sprite Multiplexing

**Technical implementation**: Once VIC-II completes drawing a sprite (after scanline Y+21), the same physical sprite can be repositioned and redrawn. This maps one physical sprite definition to multiple logical sprite instances across different scanlines.

**Mechanism**:

- VIC-II fetches sprite data during raster lines Y to Y+20 (21 lines)
- After line Y+20 completes, sprite registers ($D000-$D00F, $D015, $D027-$D02E) can be modified
- Same sprite pointer ($07F8-$07FF) reused by updating position/colour for next instance
- Raster IRQ at Y+21 triggers repositioning code
- Typical: 20-24 multiplexed sprites achievable with careful timing

**Requirements**:

- Precise raster interrupt timing (see c64://graphics/vic/spec)
- Fast register updates (< 63 cycles between sprite positions)
- Pre-calculated Y-coordinate tables for performance

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Multicolour vs Hires Sprites -->
### Multicolour vs Hires Sprites

**Hires (default)**:

- 24×21 pixels, one colour per sprite
- Better detail and sharpness
- Ideal for detailed characters or objects

**Multicolour**:

- 12×21 effective resolution (2 bits per pixel)
- 4 colours: background, sprite colour, shared 1, shared 2
- Better for colourful, less detailed objects
- Enable via bit in `$D01C`

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Priorities -->
### Sprite Priorities

- Sprites 0-7 have priority order (0 = front, 7 = back)
- Sprite-to-background priority controlled by `$D01B`
- Sprite-to-sprite collisions detected via `$D01E`
- Sprite-to-background collisions via `$D01F`

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Not Appearing -->
### Sprite Not Appearing

1. Check sprite enable bit in `$D015`
2. Verify sprite pointer at `$07F8-$07FF`
3. Confirm sprite data is in correct memory location
4. Check X/Y coordinates are on screen (0-320, 0-200)
5. Verify sprite colour is different from background

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Charset Not Displaying -->
### Charset Not Displaying

1. Confirm charset is at 2KB boundary
2. Check VIC-II bank selection (default is bank 0)
3. Verify `$D018` charset pointer bits
4. Ensure characters are POKEd to screen memory
5. Check that BASIC/KERNAL ROMs aren't blocking access

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Sprite Flicker -->
### Sprite Flicker

1. Reduce number of active sprites
2. Use sprite multiplexing carefully
3. Synchronize updates with raster beam
4. Consider double-buffering techniques

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Using render_sprite -->
### Using render_sprite

```javascript
await callTool("c64_graphics", {
  op: "render_sprite",
  sprite: "base64-encoded-63-bytes",
  x: 160,           // Center horizontally
  y: 100,           // Center vertically  
  color: 1,         // White
  multicolour: false
})
```

The tool:

- Validates 63-byte sprite format
- Writes sprite data directly into RAM
- Handles sprite pointer and VIC-II register setup
- Returns structured metadata for follow-up operations

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Memory Safety -->
### Memory Safety


When working with sprites and charsets:

1. Use memory ranges documented in c64://memory/map
2. Avoid BASIC program area ($0801-$9FFF) unless controlling it
3. Preserve zero page ($0000-$00FF) and stack ($0100-$01FF)
4. Use `c64_memory` with `op: "read"` and `op: "write"` for safe access

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Simple Sprite Display -->
### Simple Sprite Display

1. Prepare 24×21 sprite bitmap
2. Call `c64_graphics` with `op: "render_sprite"` and sprite data
3. Tool writes sprite data and patches VIC-II state automatically
4. Use `c64_memory` with `op: "read_screen"` to verify appearance
5. Optionally call `c64_memory` with `op: "write"` to adjust position/colour

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Custom Charset Installation -->
### Custom Charset Installation

1. Design character set (full or partial)
2. Encode to 8-byte-per-char format
3. Use `c64_memory` with `op: "write"` to copy the charset to $2000
4. POKE $D018 to point VIC-II at new charset
5. Use `c64_program` with `op: "upload_run_basic"` to test character display
6. Verify with `c64_memory` and `op: "read_screen"`

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Animated Sprite Sequence -->
### Animated Sprite Sequence

1. Create multiple sprite frames (3-8 frames typical)
2. Upload all frames to consecutive memory locations
3. Generate BASIC program that cycles sprite pointer
4. Use raster timing for smooth animation
5. Verify frame timing with `c64_memory` and `op: "read"` checks

records.name: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/sprite-charset-best-practices.md#Best Practices Summary -->
## Best Practices Summary

1. **Plan Memory Layout**: Map out sprite and charset locations before coding
2. **Test Incrementally**: Display one sprite/char before adding more
3. **Use Tools**: Leverage `c64_graphics` with `op: "render_sprite"` and `c64_memory` operations
4. **Document State**: Note which sprites/chars are active
5. **Handle Errors**: Check return values and screen output
6. **Optimize Last**: Get it working, then optimize if needed
7. **Verify Hardware**: Test on real C64 or accurate emulator
8. **Read Resources**: Consult c64://graphics/vic/spec for register details

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#MOS 6567/6569 VIC-II Quick Reference -->
# MOS 6567/6569 VIC-II Quick Reference

Source: <https://www.zimmers.net/cbmpics/cbm/c64/vic-ii.txt>

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#System Overview -->
## System Overview

- Core chips: 6510 CPU (NMOS, ~1.02 MHz NTSC / ~0.985 MHz PAL), VIC-II (6567 NTSC / 6569 PAL, later 8562/8565), SID 6581, two CIA 6526, 64 KB DRAM, 1 KB colour SRAM, 16 KB Kernal/BASIC ROM, 4 KB character ROM.
- VIC-II features: 40x25 text matrix, 320x200 or 160x200 bitmap, eight 24x21 sprites, 16 fixed colours, DMA/refresh master, light-pen input, IRQ generation.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Key 6510 Signals -->
## Key 6510 Signals

- `phi2`: Two-phase system clock; VIC drives phase 1 (low), CPU drives phase 2 (high).
- `R/W`: Bus direction (1 read, 0 write).
- `IRQ`, `NMI`: Interrupt inputs (VIC connects to IRQ).
- `RDY`: Halts CPU on reads when low (asserted via VIC BA).
- `AEC`: Tri-states CPU address bus when low (driven by VIC).
- `P0..P5`: On-chip port (DDR $0000, data $0001) controlling LORAM, HIRAM, CHAREN, cassette lines.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Switching character sets -->
### Switching character sets

- Via control codes: `CHR$(142)` (set 1), `CHR$(14)` (set 2)
- Via register: **$D018 (53272)** selects screen base (upper nybble, ×1 KB) and character base (lower nybble, ×2 KB; bit 0 ignored). Typical values: **21** (set 1) and **23** (set 2).
- Keyboard: **SHIFT + Commodore** toggles sets.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Rendering rules -->
### Rendering rules

- Each glyph = **8 rows × 1 byte/row**, **MSB = leftmost pixel**. Bit **1 = foreground** (per-cell color at **$D800–$DBE7**), **0 = background**.
- **Reverse-video:** characters **128–255** are reverse images of **0–127** in ROM sets.
- **Multicolor char mode:** pixels are **bit-pairs** (4 wide pixels/row). Colors: `00`=background ($D021), `01`=$D022, `10`=$D023, `11`=per-character color ($D800–$DBE7, colors 0–7). Enable multicolor via **$D011 bit 4** and color interpretation via **$D016 bit 4**; hires/multicolor can mix per cell (color RAM bit 3).

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Custom character sets in RAM -->
### Custom character sets in RAM

- **Alignment:** base address must be **2 KB-aligned** and within the **same 16 KB VIC bank** as screen RAM.
- **ROM-shadowed gaps:** VIC cannot see RAM charsets at **$1000, $1800, $9000, $9800** (ROM overlays).
- **Accessing ROM by CPU:** set **CHAREN** (I/O port at **$01**, bit 2 = 0) to map ROM at **$D000–$DFFF** for copying to RAM.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Bus Arbitration -->
## Bus Arbitration

- VIC issues a read every phase-1 slot (c/g/p/s/refresh/idle access types).
- Character pointer fetches cost 40 extra phase-2 cycles during bad lines; sprite data consumes 2 phase-2 cycles per active sprite line.
- BA drops three cycles before takeover; AEC follows low three cycles later so CPU finishes up to three writes.
- CPU stalls only on reads; writes continue until RDY is sampled on the next read.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Display Geometry -->
## Display Geometry

- Screen rendered line by line; 8 pixels per CPU cycle.
- Display window fixed centrally while borders mask surrounding area.
- `RSEL` (bit 3 of $d011): 24 rows (192 px, raster $37-$f6) or 25 rows (200 px, raster $33-$fa).
- `CSEL` (bit 3 of $d016): 38 columns (304 px, X $1f-$14e) or 40 columns (320 px, X $18-$157).
- `XSCROLL[2:0]` and `YSCROLL[2:0]`: fine scroll 0-7 pixels.
- Cycle/line metrics: 6569 PAL (63 cycles, 312 lines, 284 visible, IRQ reference X=$194, visible X $1e0-$17c); 6567R56A NTSC (64 cycles, 262 lines, 234 visible, IRQ X=$19c, visible X $1e8-$184); 6567R8 NTSC (65 cycles, 263 lines, 235 visible, IRQ X=$19c, visible X $1e9-$18c).

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Bad Lines and Counters -->
## Bad Lines and Counters

- Bad line condition: during a phi0 falling edge, raster between $30 and $f7 inclusive, low three bits equal `YSCROLL`, and `DEN` was set at least once in raster line $30.
- On a bad line the VIC pulls BA low from cycle 12, keeps AEC low from cycle 15, and performs 40 c-fetches in cycles 15-54 (phase 2).
- Internal counters: `VC` (10-bit), `VCBASE` (10-bit), `RC` (3-bit), `VMLI` (6-bit index into the 40x12 buffer).
  - Cycle 14 phase 1: `VC <- VCBASE`, `VMLI` reset; if bad line, `RC <- 0`.
  - Each g-fetch in display state increments `VC` and `VMLI`.
  - Cycle 58 phase 1: if `RC == 7`, sequencer idles and `VCBASE <- VC`; otherwise `RC++`.
- Idle state fetches from $3fff (or $39ff when ECM=1) with video matrix bits forced to 0.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Memory Access Types per Raster Line -->
## Memory Access Types per Raster Line

- `c`: video matrix + colour RAM  (12-bit).
- `g`: character/bitmap byte (8-bit) or idle fetch ($3fff/$39ff).
- `p`: sprite pointer (one per sprite each line).
- `s`: sprite data (three bytes per active sprite line, immediately after pointer).
- `r`: DRAM refresh (five accesses using REF counter).
- `i`: idle access to $3fff.
- Order is hard-wired; bad lines insert 40 consecutive `c` slots, and active sprites add `s` slots right after their pointer cycle.
records.origin: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Memory Access Types per Raster Line

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Border Logic -->
## Border Logic

- Two flip-flops: main border (controls border colour) and vertical border (gates sequencer output).
- Comparators per axis use RSEL/CSEL thresholds: horizontal $1f/$14f (38 cols) or $18/$158 (40 cols); vertical $37/$f7 (24 rows) or $33/$fb (25 rows).
- Rules: reaching right edge sets main border; left edge clears it if vertical flip-flop reset; vertical flip-flop set at bottom or when left edge meets top/bottom; DEN must be 1 to clear vertical flip-flop.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Display Enable (DEN) -->
## Display Enable (DEN)

- Clearing bit 4 of $d011 suppresses bad lines and keeps vertical border set (screen becomes full border colour).
- Re-enabling mid-frame (with YSCROLL=0) can cause DMA Delay when line $30 becomes a late bad line.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Light-Pen -->
## Light-Pen

- Negative edge on `LP` latches beam into $d013/$d014 (8-bit each; horizontal resolution is two pixels).
- Only first trigger per frame is captured; reset occurs during vertical blank.
- `LP` shares CIA1 keyboard matrix bit (port B bit 4), permitting software-triggered latching for timing.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Interrupts -->
## Interrupts

| Bit | Latch ($d019) | Enable ($d01a) | Trigger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | IRST | ERST | Raster compare hits programmed line (checked cycle 0, cycle 1 for line 0). |
| 1 | IMBC | EMBC | Sprite pixel overlaps foreground graphics pixel. |
| 2 | IMMC | EMMC | Two or more sprites output non-transparent pixels simultaneously. |
| 3 | ILP | ELP | Negative edge on light-pen input. |

- Write 1 to any asserted latch bit to clear; bit 7 mirrors IRQ line state.
- VIC asserts IRQ while any enabled latch bit remains set; CPU must clear before exiting handler (level-sensitive).

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#DRAM Refresh -->
## DRAM Refresh

- Five refresh reads per raster line via 8-bit REF counter (reset to $ff in line 0, decremented each refresh access).
- Refresh addresses: $3fff, $3ffe, $3ffd, $3ffc, $3ffb in line 0, then continue downward, wrapping every 256 refreshes.

records.name: data/graphics/vic-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/graphics/vic-spec.md#Notable Effects -->
## Notable Effects

- Hyperscreen: toggle CSEL/RSEL so comparisons never match (e.g. switch RSEL at raster 248-250) to disable borders and expose idle graphics or sprites.
- FLD (Flexible Line Distance): adjust YSCROLL to delay bad lines; controls line spacing and enables large downward scroll without memory moves.
- FLI (Flexible Line Interpretation): force bad line each raster (write YSCROLL after cycle 14) to reload colour data per line; requires cycling VM bits; first three fetches read $ff causing left-side stripes.
- Linecrunch: clear bad line condition before cycle 14 so RC stays 7 and `VCBASE` jumps by 40; collapses a text line into one raster and speeds upward scroll.
- Doubled lines: assert bad line late (cycles 54-57) so RC wraps to 0 and same line renders twice.
- DMA Delay: create bad line while sequencer idle (cycle 15-53). Initial three fetches see $ff or CPU opcode low nibble; VC misalignment shifts display horizontally without copying data.
- Sprite stretching: toggle `MxYE` around cycle 16 to repeat or skip line increments; manipulating `MCBASE` permits arbitrary vertical scaling or double rendering.

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Commodore 64 CIA Specification -->
# Commodore 64 CIA Specification

> Purpose: Single source of truth for CIA hardware on the C64 (LLM/MCP).  
> Companion specs: `io-spec.md` (system I/O topology, IEC/tape/ports), `data/printer/printer-spec.md` (printers).  
> Notes: Do **not** duplicate I/O details here—refer to `io-spec.md`. This file defines *exact CIA semantics*. Where sources disagree, this merged spec defers to the attached “Mapping the C64 CIA” and the C64 Programmer’s Reference Guide.

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Overview -->
## Overview

- **Chips:** 2× MOS **6526/6526A/8521** (functionally equivalent for C64 use).  
- **Address blocks:** **CIA1** `$DC00–$DC0F` (mirrored every 16 bytes to `$DCFF`), **CIA2** `$DD00–$DD0F` (mirrored to `$DDFF`).  
- **Core units:** Ports **PA/PB (8+8)**, **Timers A/B (16‑bit)**, **TOD clock+alarm (BCD)**, **Serial shift (SDR)**, **ICR**.  
- **System wiring:** CIA1 → **/IRQ**; CIA2 → **/NMI**. `FLAG` inputs: **CIA1** (cassette READ), **CIA2** (user port pin B).  
- **Electrical:** Port bits are open‑collector with pull‑ups; CMOS‑compatible; CNT/SP serial pins present on user port.  
- **Defaults after init:** CIA1 `DDRA=$FF` (PA out), `DDRB=$00` (PB in); CIA2 `DDRA=$3F` (bits 6–7 in), `DDRB=$00` (in).  
- **Cross‑refs:** IEC bus, user port pins, datasette lines, VIC bank select, joystick/paddles/key scan → see `io-spec.md`.

| Address | Decimal | Name | Function / Bits (compact) |
|:-------:|:-------:|:-----|:---------------------------|
| `$DC0E` | 56334 | **CRA** | **Timer A ctrl**/**serial/TOD**: **b0** start; **b1** PB6 enable; **b2** PB6 mode (1 toggle / 0 pulse); **b3** one‑shot; **b4** force load; **b5** count src (1=CNT / 0=Φ2); **b6** SDR dir (1 out); **b7** TOD freq (1=50 Hz/0=60 Hz). |
| `$DC0F` | 56335 | **CRB** | **Timer B ctrl/TOD sel**: **b0** start; **b1** PB7 enable; **b2** PB7 mode; **b3** one‑shot; **b4** force load; **b6..b5** mode: `00`=Φ2, `01`=CNT, `10`=TA underflow, `11`=TA underflow gated by CNT; **b7** TOD write target (1=ALARM/0=TIME). |

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Timers (A/B) — Operation -->
## Timers (A/B) — Operation

- **16‑bit down‑counters** with separate **latches** (write low→high). **Start** or **CRA/CRB b4** forces latch→counter.  
- **Clock sources:** Φ2 (system cycles) or **CNT** pulses; **Timer B** can count **Timer A underflows**, gated by CNT if mode `11`.  
- **Underflow:** Sets ICR bit (and asserts IRQ/NMI). Optional **PB6/PB7** **pulse** (b2=0) or **toggle** (b2=1). **b3=1** one‑shot; else auto‑reload.  
- **Readback:** Reads return current counter; device internally manages proper two‑byte read behavior.  
- **Typical OS setup:** CIA1 Timer A ≈ 1/60 s IRQ; tape I/O repurposes CIA1 timers; CIA2 timers often used by RS‑232.

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Pinout (logical summary) -->
## Pinout (logical summary)

`PA0–PA7`, `PB0–PB7` (parallel I/O); `/PC` (handshake pulse after PB access; only CIA2 connected externally); `SP` (serial data), `CNT` (count/serial clock); `FLAG` (neg‑edge IRQ/NMI input); `/IRQ` (CIA1), `/NMI` (CIA2); `RS0–RS3` (reg select); `DB0–DB7`; `R/W`; `/CS`; `/RES`; `Φ2`; `Vcc`; `Vss`.  
User‑port mapping for CIA2 PRB and PRA b2 is defined in `io-spec.md` (pin letters C..N).

records.name: data/io/cia-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/cia-spec.md#Behavior Notes / Gotchas (LLM hints) -->
## Behavior Notes / Gotchas (LLM hints)

- **Keyboard scan vs Joystick 1:** Shared on **PRB**; keyscan can misread joystick state and vice‑versa. Gate scan or prefer **Port 2** for games.  
- **Paddles:** Buttons via CIA **bits 2–3**; *positions* via **SID** POTX/POTY; select port with **PRA b7/b6**.  
- **Mirroring:** Access any `$xx00–$xx0F` alias in the `$xx10–$xxFF` window; use base addresses for clarity.  
- **VIC bank:** Use **CIA2 PRA[1:0]**; update VIC `$D018` pointers accordingly (see `io-spec.md`).  
- **Datasette:** READ→CIA1 **FLAG** (ICR b4); MOTOR/WRITE/SENSE via CPU `$0001` (see `io-spec.md`).

## 2. Device Addressing & KERNAL I/O

- **Device numbers (IEC):** Printers **4–7** (convention: 4), Storage **8–30** (convention: first disk **8**). Keyboard=0, Tape=1, RS‑232=2, Screen=3. Secondary addresses distinguish channels on same device.
- **Bus role:** C64 is IEC **master**; commands: **LISTEN**, **TALK**, **UNLISTEN**, **UNTALK**, **OPEN/CLOSE channel**, with **ATN** controlling command vs data phases.
- **Key KERNAL entry points:** `OPEN`, `CLOSE`, `CHKIN`, `CHKOUT`, `CLRCHN`, `CHRIN`, `CHROUT`, `LOAD`, `SAVE` (see pagetable KERNAL reference for exact call vectors/regs).

---

records.name: data/io/io-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/io-spec.md#4. Datasette (Tape) I/O -->
## 4. Datasette (Tape) I/O

- **CPU Port ($0001):** **bit5 MOTOR** (0=on), **bit4 SENSE** (0=key pressed), **bit3 WRITE** (tape out). Direction via $0000.
- **Read:** Cassette **READ → CIA1 /FLAG** (edge‑sensitive, falling only). **ICR bit4** set on edge; enable IRQ via ICR mask.
- **Implication:** Can **toggle** write/motor; **cannot level‑poll** read—only edges—so loaders measure inter‑edge timing (often with CIA timers).

---

records.name: data/io/io-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/io-spec.md#6. Joysticks, Lightpen, Paddles -->
## 6. Joysticks, Lightpen, Paddles

- **Joysticks:** Digital switches, active‑low. **Port 1 → CIA1 PRB[0..4]**, **Port 2 → CIA1 PRA[0..4]** (see `cia-spec.md` mapping). Joystick‑keyboard contention exists on Port 1.
- **Lightpen:** Routed via VIC /LP; also appears as “fire” on CIA1. Use VIC registers for position latch. (Mapping note: see `cia-spec.md`.)
- **Paddles:** Analog via **SID POTX/POTY**; channel selection via **CIA1 PRA[6:7]** to choose control port.

---

records.name: data/io/io-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/io-spec.md#7. User Port (Rear Edge Connector) -->
## 7. User Port (Rear Edge Connector)

- **Logical:** **CIA2 PRB (PB0–PB7)** as general‑purpose digital I/O; configure with **DDRB**; read/write via **PRB**. KERNAL also provides RS‑232 routines mapping PB pins.
- **RS‑232:** TTL‑level via User Port; needs level shifting (e.g., MAX232). High‑speed bit‑bangers (e.g., UP9600) leverage CIA timing/interrupts.

---

records.name: data/io/io-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/io-spec.md#9. VIC Bank Select (Memory Windows) -->
## 9. VIC Bank Select (Memory Windows)

- **CIA2 PRA[1:0]:** **00=$C000–FFFF**, **01=$8000–BFFF**, **10=$4000–7FFF**, **11=$0000–3FFF (default)**. Controls VIC’s addressable 16 KiB bank. (Use with VIC memory pointers).

---

records.name: data/io/io-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/io/io-spec.md#10. Recommended Access Patterns (Summary) -->
## 10. Recommended Access Patterns (Summary)

- **Prefer KERNAL** for disk/printer where compatibility matters; switch to custom IEC only for speed‑critical paths.
- **Keyboard:** CIA1 column‑by‑column scan; handle Port‑1 joystick aliasing.
- **Tape:** Control motor/write via $0001; measure **FLAG** edges via CIA1 ICR.
- **User Port:** Set DDRB and use PRB; add RS‑232 level shifting if interfacing to standard serial.
- **Expansion Port:** Memory‑mapped by cartridge; coordinate with bank switching and KERNAL vectors.

---

# Low Memory Pages 0–3 (Zero Page, Stack, System Work Areas)

> Scope: **$0000–$03FF (0–1023)**: Zero page (BASIC + KERNAL vars), page-1 stack, page-2 system buffers/tables, page-3 vectors + **cassette (tape) buffer**.

# SID File Structure (PSID/RSID) — Concise Overview

This guide summarizes the High Voltage SID Collection (HVSC) "PSID file format" header used by classic SID tunes. A SID file consists of:

- A header containing metadata and playback parameters
- The actual 6502 machine code and data that the player runs on the C64

You can play a SID file on a connected device with the MCP tool `c64_sound` and `op: "play_sid_file"`.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-file-structure.md#Extended header (versions 2–4) -->
## Extended header (versions 2–4)

These versions append more detail for environment and chip configuration.

- +76 — flags (uint32): bitfield
  - b0: 0 = built-in player, 1 = Compute! player
  - b1: 0 = C64-compatible PSID, 1 = PlaySID-specific/C64 BASIC
  - b2–b3 (video): `01`=PAL, `10`=NTSC, `11`=Both, `00`=Unknown
  - b4–b5 (primary SID model): `00`=unknown, `01`=6581, `10`=8580, `11`=both
  - b6–b7 (second SID model): same encoding (v3+)
  - b8–b9 (third SID model): same encoding (v4)
  - Remaining bits reserved (set to 0)
- +78 — startPage (uint8): high byte of a free memory page for a music driver; `0` means free outside data block, `0xFF` means none
- +79 — pageLength (uint8): number of contiguous pages available starting at `startPage`
- +7A — secondSIDAddress (uint8): `0x2x` → second SID at `$D2x0`, etc. (v3+)
- +7B — thirdSIDAddress (uint8): third SID address like above (v4)
- +7C — data start (beginning of machine code and data)

Notes:

- Version number loosely correlates with multi-SID usage: v2 single-SID, v3 dual-SID, v4 triple-SID.
- PAL vs NTSC differences and SID model (6581/8580) materially affect sound; consult `flags`.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-file-structure.md#Timing and interrupts -->
## Timing and interrupts

- `speed` determines whether playback uses VBlank (VIC raster IRQ) or CIA1 timer.
- In RSID, VIC raster is generally not to be assumed; rely on the player-installed timing per header hints.

records.name: data/sound/sid-file-structure.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-file-structure.md#Song length database (Songlengths.md5) -->
## Song length database (Songlengths.md5)

SID files do not embed duration. HVSC ships a `Songlengths.md5` database mapping each file’s MD5 to a track length:

- Format: INI-like: a header line `[database]`, then repeated groups of a commented filename line (starts with `;`) and a line with `MD5 = mm:ss[.ms]`.
- To obtain a length: compute MD5 of the full SID file (header + data), look up the matching entry, parse minutes/seconds (and optional milliseconds).

### 3. Proper ADSR Envelope

- **Attack/Decay (54277)**: `17` = fast attack (1), slow decay (7)
- **Sustain/Release (54278)**: `240` = high sustain (15), no release (0)
- **Effect**: Creates natural-sounding note onset and sustain

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Filter Block -->
## Filter Block

- **Cutoff:** $D415 + $D416 (11 bits).  
- **Resonance / Routing:** $D417.  
- **Mode / Volume:** $D418 → LP/BP/HP bits + master volume.  
- **Differences:** 6581 = nonlinear; 8580 = more accurate.

---

records.name: data/sound/sid-spec.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sid-spec.md#Famous Effects -->
## Famous Effects

**Arpeggio** – Cycle chord intervals (e.g. 0,+4,+7) each tick by rewriting FREQ.  
**Vibrato** – Small sinusoidal offset of FREQ each tick (software LFO).  
**PWM** – Periodic variation of pulse-width for animated tone.  
**Filter Sweep** – Ramp cutoff ($D415/$D416) and/or resonance ($D417).  
**Hard Restart** – Clear GATE early, optionally TEST=1 to reset osc; next tick set ADSR + GATE=1 for tight attack.  
**Sync / Ring-Mod** – Enable SYNC or RING bits in CTRL to tie oscillators.  
**Digi Playback** – Rapid writes to $D418 volume simulate 4-bit PCM DAC (~4–8 kHz).

---

# SIDWAVE Format Specification

This document defines **SIDWAVE**, a declarative format for describing structured C64 SID compositions.
SIDWAVE files are authored in YAML (or JSON) and compiled by the MCP server (`music_compile_and_play`) into a `.PRG` or `.SID` (PSID v2) binary with a built-in frame-based player.

Pipeline:

LLM → SIDWAVE (YAML) → MCP compiler → PRG or PSID → C64 / Ultimate / VICE playback

---

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#File and Schema Conventions -->
## File and Schema Conventions

- **Format name:** SIDWAVE
- **File suffix:** `.sidwave.yaml` (or `.sid.yaml` for brevity)
- **Version field:** `sidwave: 1.0`
- **Schema file:** `sidwave.schema.json`
- **Serialization:** YAML 1.2 or JSON

Unknown fields, unknown pattern names, invalid notes and out-of-range values are rejected with an error that names the path, for example `Invalid SIDWAVE at $.timeline[1].layers.v2: pattern "X" is not defined for voice 2 (known: B)`.

> YAML pitfall: inside a flow map, a bare `-` starts a list. Write silent layers as `v2: "-"`, not `v2: -`.

---

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisgleissner/c64bridge/refs/heads/main/data/sound/sidwave.schema.json -->
# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/chrisgleissner/c64bridge/refs/heads/main/data/sound/sidwave.schema.json
sidwave: 1.0
title: "Echoes of Tomorrow"
author: "Generated by MCP"
tempo: 92
mode: PAL
global_fx:
  reverb_sim: { depth: 0.3, delay_frames: 3 }
  filter_env: { cutoff_base: 1800, sweep: -800, speed: 12 }

voices:
  - id: 1
    name: LeadPad
    waveform: sawtooth
    adsr: [4, 2, 10, 3]
    patterns:
      A:
        length: 16
        motif: "Cmin9 pad motif"
        transpositions: [0, 5, 7]
        fx:
          vibrato: { depth: 0.25, rate: 5, delay: 10 }
          filter_mod: { sweep: "+500 over 8 beats" }

  - id: 2
    name: ArpLayer
    waveform: pulse
    pulse_width: 0.3
    patterns:
      B:
        type: arpeggio
        notes: [C3, Eb3, G3, Bb3]
        frame_rate: 2
        fx:
          pwm_sweep: { speed: 1, depth: 0.2 }

  - id: 3
    name: Bass
    waveform: triangle
    patterns:
      C:
        groove: [C1, C1, C1, G0]
        fx:
          slide: { depth: 2, speed: 3 }

timeline:
  - section: "Intro"
    bars: 16
    layers: { v1: A, v2: "-", v3: C }
  - section: "Build"
    bars: 32
    layers: { v1: A↑, v2: B, v3: C }
  - section: "Drift"
    bars: 48
    layers: { v1: A↓, v2: B, v3: C }
  - section: "Fade"
    bars: 32
    layers: { v1: A–, v2: "-", v3: "-" }
```

---

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Song Fields -->
## Song Fields

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `sidwave` | Format version, `1.0`. |
| `title`, `author` | Written to the PSID header (Latin-1, 32 characters). |
| `tempo` | Beats (quarter notes) per minute, 30–220. Default 100. |
| `mode` | `PAL` (985248 Hz clock, 50.12 frames/s) or `NTSC` (1022727 Hz clock, 59.83 frames/s). Default `PAL`. |
| `length_bars` | Optional song length. Shorter than the timeline truncates it; longer repeats the timeline from the start. Default: the sum of the timeline's bars. |
| `global_fx` | `reverb_sim` and `filter_env`, described below. |
| `voices` | One to three voices with ids 1–3. Voices that are not declared stay silent. |
| `timeline` | Sections played in order. The song loops forever after the last section. |

The legacy shape with a `song: { title, author, tempo, mode, length_bars, global_fx }` block next to `voices` and `timeline` is also accepted.

Time is 4/4: a bar has four beats. The player runs once per video frame of a real C64 (50.1245 Hz on PAL, 59.8262 Hz on NTSC). Every onset is placed on the nearest frame of its exact time (`beat × 60 / tempo × frame rate`), so long songs do not drift; individual notes may be one frame longer or shorter than the average.

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Voices -->
## Voices

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | SID voice 1, 2 or 3. |
| `name` | Label only. |
| `waveform` | `pulse`, `sawtooth` (`saw`), `triangle` (`tri`) or `noise`. Default `pulse`. |
| `pulse_width` | Pulse duty cycle: a fraction (0 < x ≤ 1, e.g. `0.3`) or a 12-bit value 1–4094. Default 2048 (50 %). |
| `adsr` | `[attack, decay, sustain, release]`, each 0–15 (SID register nibbles). Default `[2, 2, 10, 3]`. |
| `patterns` | Named patterns used by the timeline. |

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Global effects (`global_fx`) -->
## Global effects (`global_fx`)

| Effect | Fields | Behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `filter_env` | `cutoff_base` (0–2047), `sweep` (±2047), `speed` (beats per one-way sweep), `resonance` (0–15, default 8), `type` (`lowpass` default, `bandpass`, `highpass`), `voices` (default all) | Enables the SID filter for the listed voices. The cutoff moves back and forth between `cutoff_base` and `cutoff_base + sweep`, each direction taking `speed` beats. Without `sweep`/`speed` the cutoff stays at `cutoff_base`. The sweep restarts from `cutoff_base` each time the song loops, so every pass sounds the same. `filter_mod` offsets are added on top. |
| `reverb_sim` | `depth` (0 < x ≤ 1), `delay_frames` (1–50) | In sections that leave a voice free, the lowest free voice echoes the lowest sounding voice `delay_frames` later, with its sustain level scaled by `depth`. The SID has no per-voice volume, so the echo's attack peak is as loud as the original; only the sustained part is quieter. Sections that use all three voices have no echo. |

Without `filter_env`, a `filter_mod` uses a low-pass filter with cutoff 1024 and resonance 8 as its base. The SID has a single filter, so all routed voices share it; when several patterns with `filter_mod` start at once, the most recent start sets the ramp.

---

records.name: data/sound/sidwave.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Player -->
## Player

The compiler arranges the timeline into per-voice note events and encodes them as compact command streams (note, instrument, wait, gate-off, hard restart, sustain, volume, filter ramp, loop). A 6502 player reads these streams once per video frame and computes per-frame effects itself.

- **Hard restart:** two frames before every new note the voice's gate is released and its ADSR is set to zero, so each note starts a fresh envelope (this avoids the SID's ADSR delay bug). A note therefore sounds with the gate on until two frames before the next note, so every note needs at least 3 frames (one sounding frame plus the hard restart). Entries shorter than 3 frames are rejected, which limits very short entries at fast tempos (for example 1/16 notes are fine at 220 BPM, 1/32 notes are not). A note that is cut to fewer than 3 frames by the end of a section is dropped.
- **Gate:** a rest releases the gate at its start, so the note decays with its release rate.
- **Instruments:** each voice/pattern/effect combination becomes an instrument with its own ADSR, waveform, pulse settings, vibrato, arpeggio table, slide and filter routing (up to 63).
- **Memory:** the program loads at $0801 and must end below $D000 (about 50 KB). Very long, dense songs are rejected with a validation error rather than truncated. The player uses zero-page bytes $FB/$FC and restores them after every call.
- **CPU time:** typical songs take 20–65 raster lines per frame (about 1,400–4,100 cycles). The worst case, all three voices starting notes with vibrato, slide, arpeggio, pulse sweep and filter ramp in the same frame, takes about 9,800 cycles (155 raster lines, half a PAL frame), mostly for the arithmetic that scales vibrato and slide to each note's pitch (an 8×8 multiply from a 1 KB table of squares).

<!-- Source: data/sound/sidwave.md#Output formats -->
### Output formats

- **PSID (`output: sid`):** PSID v2 with init at $0810, play at $0813, vertical-blank timing, and the PAL or NTSC clock flag from `mode`. The SID model is left unspecified.
- **PRG (`output: prg`):** `10 SYS2061`. The program detects whether the machine is PAL or NTSC, programs CIA 1 timer A for the song's frame rate on that clock, installs an IRQ handler, and returns to BASIC while the music plays. Pitch and tempo are therefore correct on either machine type.
  - Before returning, it moves the start of BASIC and the variable area behind the player (like `NEW` with a raised start of BASIC), so direct-mode commands, variables and new program lines work without touching the player. The compile result reports `basicFreeBytes`. A song whose PRG ends at or above $A000 leaves no BASIC memory: BASIC commands that need memory then fail with `?OUT OF MEMORY` while the music keeps playing, and the compile result carries a warning.
  - Because the KERNAL's IRQ (keyboard scan, cursor blink, jiffy clock) now runs at the song's frame rate instead of 60 Hz, `TI`/`TI$` runs about 16.5 % slow for a PAL song (0.3 % for NTSC), and key repeat and cursor blink slow down accordingly while the music plays.

# Ultimate turbo benchmark (CPU budget, badlines, sprites, I/O, REU DMA)

Measures how many CPU cycles a game really gets per frame on an Ultimate 64 or C64 Ultimate at each turbo setting, and how
fast REU DMA runs. The programs are written for the c64bridge assembler (`c64_program` op `upload_run_asm`): one call, no
toolchain. Measured results are in `results/` (`summary.md`, one JSON file per device and date). The knowledge resources
c64://ultimate/hardware, c64://ultimate/reu and c64://gamedev/architecture quote them.

Raw per-point JSON results are in the GitHub repository under data/ultimate/bench/results/; the npm package ships only results/summary.md.

Files: `turbo-cpu.asm`, `turbo-reu.asm`, `turbo-window.asm` (this directory), host script `scripts/turbo-bench.mjs`
(`npm run bench:turbo`).

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/bench/README.md#Formulas -->
### Formulas

* CPU, per point: `multiple = N x 13575 / ticks`, N = 29 x MHz. `13575` is the number of CPU cycles (at nominal timing)
  of one outer pass: `256 x (48 + 2 + 3) - 1 + 5 + 3`. Take the median over the repetitions.
* `effective 1 MHz-equivalent cycles per frame = multiple x frame_ticks` (frame_ticks 19656 PAL, 17095 NTSC; use the
  measured median from the header). Per raster line: divide by 312 (PAL) or 263 (NTSC). `multiple` is the delivered
  speed as a multiple of PHI2, for example 46.99 for the 48 MHz setting.
* Cycles lost compared with a blanked screen at the same speed: `(multiple_blank - multiple_on) x frame_ticks`.
* REU: `bytes per PHI2 tick = (32768 - 16384) / (ticks_32K - ticks_16K)` (removes start-up overhead); the 1-byte
  transfer shows that overhead (14 ticks on VICE). 1.0 means one byte per 1 MHz cycle.
* Window: the first attempt with `probe_ticks < 65536` marks the speed taking effect; its wall-clock stamp is the time
  after program start (convert ticks to ms with 985.248 PAL, 1022.7 NTSC).

`scripts/turbo-bench.mjs --decode <file>` implements exactly this for a raw 3840-byte block.

Interpretation checks: the frame-length records must read 19656 or 19657 (PAL) or 17095 or 17096 (NTSC). At 1 MHz with the
screen blanked every load must give multiple 1.0000. With the screen on at 1 MHz and `$D031` bit 7 clear, about 25 badlines
x 43 cycles are lost (about 1,080 per PAL frame). A point with an interference flag, a spread above 0.5 percent or status
`$FF` is rerun once and reported, not dropped.

Speed-mode notes: in `Manual` and `TurboEnable Bit` mode set `USE_D031 = 0` and `NOMINAL_M` to the configured speed. The
program has no liveness probe in that mode, so the first repetition runs inside the 1 MHz window after the reset; it shows
as an interference flag on the first point and the median of three repetitions is not affected. Insert a delay or discard
that point when it matters.

# Ultimate Devices: Hardware Features Visible to a C64 Program

**Summary:** Ultimate 64 (U64), Elite (MK1), Elite II and C64 Ultimate (C64U) add a CPU turbo, several SIDs, an REU, a command interface (UCI) and a runtime palette, all absent in VICE and on a stock C64: detect, then fall back. **Read when:** designing or detecting turbo, SID layout, REU/UCI, model-dependent code, Ultimate-only game features.

Marks: "(unverified)" = secondary or inferred; "measured" = 2026-11-13, Ultimate 64 Elite fw 3.15a, C64U fw 1.2.1, PAL. Firmware dates: entry into the public master; released firmware may be older, so probe, not version-check. Docs: 1541u-documentation.readthedocs.io; firmware: GideonZ/1541ultimate.

<!-- Source: data/ultimate/hardware.md#Multiple SIDs -->
## Multiple SIDs

Full control recipe, address map, mixer and detection: c64://ultimate/multisid (verified on a C64U, fw 1.2.1).

- Two UltiSID (FPGA) and two sockets; `UltiSID Range Split` `1/4 (A7,A8)` makes 8 UltiSID parts (24 voices), sockets add 1 each (10, or 12 with dual-SID chips). Items: `SID Socket 1/2 Address`, `UltiSID 1/2 Address`, `Ext DualSID Range Split`, `Auto Address Mirroring` (default Enabled: every decoder at `$D400` answers all of `$D400-$D7FF`, so all chips hear every write).
- Addresses: `Unmapped`, `$D400`..`$D7E0`, `$DE00`..`$DFE0`, steps `$20`. Keep SIDs out of `$DE00-$DFFF` (REU, UCI). Access only to mapped windows: an undecoded `$D400-$D7FF` address hangs the CPU or the device (Elite fw 3.15; assume the same on the C64U).
- Mixer: Vol/Pan per UltiSID 1, UltiSID 2, Socket 1, Socket 2; split parts share their parent's pan. The UDP audio stream carries the mixer output, so pan and volume are in it. Per-UltiSID: filter curve, resonance, combined waveforms, digi level.
- Run-time setup: UCI `LOAD_CONFIG` (fw 1.2.1 verified). Detection: UCI `GET_HWINFO` sub 1 lists the four decoders (not parts); test each mapped window with ENV3. Host: REST `GET /v1/configs/SID Addressing`, `SID Sockets Configuration`.

<!-- Source: data/ultimate/hardware.md#Detecting an Ultimate and its model -->
## Detecting an Ultimate and its model

1. UCI: read `$DF1D`, mask `$7F`, compare `$49` (`$C9` when no interrupt pending). Needs `Command Interface` enabled (default Disabled); when off it looks like no Ultimate.
2. Turbo probe: `$D031` not `$FF` = turbo registers on; `$FF` proves nothing.
3. Model: UCI IDENTIFY on target 4 answers `CONTROL TARGET V1.1`; GET_HWINFO (deprecated, `$04 $28`) returns a mixed-case product string (fold case). Measured on a C64U: GET_HWINFO reported plain "Ultimate 64", same as a 48 MHz U64; tell 48 from 64 MHz by the speed probe.
4. Host: `GET /v1/info` returns `product`, `firmware_version`, `fpga_version`, `core_version`; `c64://platform/status` reports the active backend.
5. Probe features by trying them (unknown UCI command: `21,UNKNOWN COMMAND`).

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/hardware.md#Other features -->
## Other features

- Runtime palette: UCI control commands `$51-$54` (U64-class, firmware 2026-09; check for error 21); `.vpl` fixed palette since 3.10 (c64://ultimate/uci).
- Other video items (HDMI scanlines, analog mode, `Adjust Color Clock`) are post-processing, not C64 timing. No second VIC, extra video mode or extended VIC registers; sprites, multicolour, ECM, bitmap are standard.
- `Joystick Swapper`, `Mouse Mode`, `DMA Load Mimics ID`, `Fast Reset`, `Burst Mode Patch` are config/launch settings, not program features.

records.name: data/ultimate/hardware.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/hardware.md#Case light and keyboard LEDs (C64U) -->
- Both have `LedStrip Mode` (`Off`, `Fixed Color`, `SID Music`, `Rainbow`, `Rainbow Sparkle`, `Sparkle` (case), `Default`, `Programmatic`), `LedStrip Pattern`, `Strip Intensity` 0-31, `Fixed Color` (25 hues `Red`..`White`), `Color tint`, `LedStrip SID Select`, `LedStrip Auto SID Mode`. Free RGB needs `Programmatic`.
- Per-LED colour: mode `Programmatic` in that category, then in C64 address space (a program, or REST DMA, see below):
  1. `$D037` <- `$11` once: `$D200-$D3FF` switches from VIC mirrors to the LED controllers (`$D2xx` case, `$D3xx` keyboard). Without it writes do nothing; a C64 reset clears it.
  2. Per window: `$xx00-$xxFB` LED n at 3n, 3 bytes; `$xxFE` global intensity; `$xxFF` any write latches and refreshes, send it after the colours.
  3. Byte order: keyboard **G, R, B**; case **R, G, B** (verified with `FF 00 00` and `00 FF 00`).
- No resident program needed (verified): `PUT /v1/machine:writemem?address=D037&data=11`, then `address=D300&data=<hex>` for colours and `address=D3FE&data=3000` for intensity and latch. PUT with hex in the URL takes about 17 ms and works up to 128 bytes (200 failed); POST with a body takes about 195 ms whatever the size. Each request pauses the C64 briefly. Measured: moving one LED (6 bytes plus latch, 2 requests) 30 updates/s; full frame (213 or 252 bytes, 3 requests) 13/s. A 6502 loop wrote 600 colour-plus-latch sequences in at most 4 jiffies; LED refresh rate not measured.
- Verified by camera: LED 5 red, 20 green, 40 blue, 60 white, rest off in one update; a single LED raced through all 71 keyboard and all 84 case indices in order with colours red, green, blue, yellow, cyan, magenta, white cycling; every index lit one position. Keyboard index 35 was too dim to see. Amber case plastic tints case colours.

## Pitfalls

1. Never assume turbo: check `$D031`, keep a 1 MHz path.
2. `$D030-$D03F`, `$D07A-$D0BC` are not scratch; no "index N = X MHz" beyond index 3.
3. REST memory access (`c64_memory`) stalls the CPU; can glitch timing-critical code.
4. IEC or fastloader code under a Manual speed: test first (unverified).
5. Unknown product names must not fail.

# Ultimate Devices: Multi-SID Control for Games

**Summary:** A C64 Ultimate (C64U) has two UltiSIDs (FPGA SIDs) that split into 8 independent SIDs, plus two SID sockets: 8 to 10 SIDs (24 to 30 voices), up to 12 with dual-SID chips. A game places them with a `.cfg` and UCI `LOAD_CONFIG`, writes only to mapped windows and verifies each with ENV3. Verified on a C64U, firmware 1.2.1 (two UltiSID, two ARMSID).
**Read when:** a modern C64U/Ultimate game uses more than one SID, sets SID addresses or stereo at run time, or must work with empty sockets, one or two real SIDs or SID replacements (ARMSID, ARM2SID, FPGASID, SwinSID); not on a stock C64 or in VICE.

Marks: "device" = measured on a C64U 1.2.1, PAL, 2026-11-13; "source" = public firmware repository GideonZ/1541ultimate (master of 2026-10-31, `software/u64/u64_config.cc`, `software/io/command_interface/control_target.cc`) only. The FPGA is closed source, so internal behaviour is source or device only.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/multisid.md#Mixer, pan and the audio stream -->
## Mixer, pan and the audio stream

- Store `Audio Mixer`: ten channels; the SID ones are UltiSID 1, UltiSID 2, Socket 1, Socket 2 with `Vol <name>` and `Pan <name>`; `Vol Master`. Pan is `Left 5`..`Left 1`, `Center`, `Right 1`..`Right 5`. Defaults: UltiSIDs `Center`, Socket 1 `Left 3`, Socket 2 `Right 3`.
- All parts of an UltiSID share its volume and pan. Per-part level uses `$D418` of that part: linear, independent of every other part (device: volume 8 gives 0.53, 4 gives 0.27 of volume 15; others unchanged to within 1 percent). Amplitude panning between a left part and a right part works by the level ratio (device).
- Stereo separation (device): with `Pan UltiSID 1=Left 5` and `Pan UltiSID 2=Right 5` an UltiSID 1 part is absent on the right channel (more than 95 dB down) and an UltiSID 2 part on the left.
- The UDP audio stream (`PUT /v1/streams/audio:start`, 192 stereo S16 frames per packet, 47982.89 Hz PAL) is the final mixer output: all eight parts and both sockets, with their pan and volume (device). Use it to test sound from the host.
- Level (device, sawtooth, volume 15, mixer 0 dB): one voice about 0.24 of full scale on the loud side; 12 voices on one pan side about 0.92; 24 UltiSID voices clip. Keep the sum of (volume/15 times sustain/15) per pan side at or below about 10 for saw sounds.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/multisid.md#Detection -->
## Detection

- `GET_HWINFO` (command `$28`) device 0 returns the product string (device: `C64 Ultimate`); device 1 returns a count then 5 bytes per decoder: UltiSID 1, UltiSID 2, then each enabled socket. Entry: address low, address high, `$00`, `$00`, type (2, or 3 when the mask is not `$FE` (split or mirrored), plus 128, for UltiSIDs; 4 or 5 for sockets). Device: 10-SID map gives `04 00D4.. 20D4.. 40D4.. 60D4..`. Parts, second SIDs and the chip type are not listed. REST `SID Sockets Configuration` gives `SID Detected Socket 1/2` (None, 6581, 8580, ARMSID, ARM2SID, FPGASID, SwinSID Ultimate, PDsid, SIDKick ...) for a host installer.
- ENV3 test (device: 10 windows by 10, both from the 6510 and by REST, gives the identity matrix): silence all; at window i set voice 3 to triangle or saw at a high frequency, attack 0, sustain 15, gate on, volume 15; wait two frames; read `$1C` of every mapped window: window i gives `$FF`, all others `$00`. Close the gate afterwards. OSC3 `$1B` keeps changing after the gate closes and is not a presence test. Any other window that also reads `$FF` means an overlap: fall back to a smaller map.
- Test only mapped windows. Without UCI, play as one SID at `$D400`.
- Observation (device): REST `writemem` to the Socket 1 window was, in several runs with the audio stream running, also heard on Socket 2 (6510 writes were clean in the 10 by 10 test). Check both sockets' ENV3 before trusting REST-based sound tests.

records.name: data/ultimate/multisid.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/multisid.md#Differences in sound -->
## Differences in sound

- UltiSID: filter curve per UltiSID (`8580 Lo`, `8580 Hi`, `6581`, `6581 Alt`, `U2 Low`, `U2 Mid`, `U2 High`), `Filter Resonance` `Low`/`High`, `Combined Waveforms` `6581`/`8580`, `Digis Level`, set in store `UltiSID Configuration`; both UltiSIDs can differ. Use single waveforms and filters that sound right across curves.
- Sockets are real or emulated chips with their own filter, DC and noise; device: the two ARMSID differ by about ten times in master-volume click and by two times in the level of the same triangle.
- Master volume ($D418) steps click: one step about 900 units (UltiSID) to 1400 (ARMSID in one socket) of 32767, 0 to 15 about 0.4 to 0.6 of full scale on the loud side (device). Step volume by one at most, only on silent chips.
- Same-frequency unison on two chips: two UltiSID parts add to 0.71 of the sum for triangle, saw and pulse; an UltiSID against an ARMSID gave 0.32 (triangle), 0.74 (saw) and 0.99 (pulse), repeatably (device). Do not rely on unison for level; detune slightly. For width instead: the same 440 Hz tri/saw/pulse on voice 1 of four chips panned apart (Left 3, Center, Left 3, Right 3) gave a slowly moving, spacious beating field, judged atmospheric by ear (device): stereo movement without modulation.
- Not measured: ADSR delay bug on UltiSID and ARMSID, filter range of split parts, cost of socket writes (sockets sit behind the 1 MHz bridge, source). Plan for note starts up to two frames late.

# REU (RAM Expansion Unit) on Ultimate Devices

**Summary:** Ultimate devices emulate a 1750-compatible REU (128 KB to 16 MB) in SDRAM, registers at `$DF00-$DF0A`. DMA stalls the CPU, REU contents survive C64 resets, and the REU is disabled by default. No REST endpoint writes REU memory: data gets in through boot-time preload, UCI LOAD_REU from game code, or a stash stub. Games use it for level data, charset/sprite/bitmap streaming and sample storage.
**Read when:** storing or streaming game data via the REU, writing DMA routines, or deciding how to load an REU image.

Marks: "(unverified)" = inferred or single secondary source; "Measured" = benchmark. Related: c64://ultimate/uci (LOAD_REU commands), c64://ultimate/hardware (turbo, `$DE00-$DFFF` map), c64://memory/map, c64://io/spec.

records.name: data/ultimate/reu.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/reu.md#Timing, stall, size, wrap -->
- The CPU is halted for the whole transfer (no wait loop needed; the status is valid on the next instruction). A raster/CIA IRQ falling inside it fires late. Menu freeze pauses a running transfer.
- Measured 2026-11-13 on Ultimate 64 Elite fw 3.15a and C64U fw 1.2.1, PAL, 16 MB REU; rerun: c64://ultimate/hardware#rerun or c64://ultimate/bench. The rate depends on the CPU turbo setting (1 byte per microsecond holds only at 1-3 MHz). Bytes per microsecond, stash / fetch, screen blanked: 1 MHz 0.99 / 0.99, 2 MHz 1.97 / 1.97, 3 MHz 2.96 / 2.93. Top speed: U64 48 MHz 5.1 / 3.6, C64U 64 MHz 7.8 / 4.3. Not monotonic: U64 4 MHz fetch 2.0 and 6 MHz stash 3.0; C64U 10 MHz stash 4.9 against 7.7 at 8 MHz. Floors from 6 MHz up: U64 3.0 / 2.6, C64U 4.9 / 2.9.
- Screen on with badlines costs about 5 percent of the rate;none with `$D031` bit 7 set. Each transfer has a fixed overhead of 3 to 15 PHI2 ticks (1-byte transfers: 15 at 1 MHz, 3 at top speed).
- At top speed a CPU store loop (derived: about 12 B/us at 64 MHz) outruns REU stash: do not DMA-fill then.
- **512 KB wrap:** on builds without the extended registers, and in VICE, a transfer that crosses a 512 KB boundary (REU address multiple of `$080000`) wraps inside that block. Rule: split every DMA so `(addr & $07FFFF) + len <= $080000`; guard length 0 (it means 64 KB). Extended builds mask the address to the configured size instead.

records.name: data/ultimate/reu.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/reu.md#Timing, stall, size, wrap -->
- **Size detection** (no UCI command reports it): fetch the byte at REU offset 0, stash back `a^$A5`, fetch again (no REU if it does not hold; restore it). Then for s = 64 KB, 128 KB, ... 8 MB: save bytes at 0 and s, write `a^$A5` at 0 and `a^$5A` at s; if offset 0 now holds the second value the REU aliases at s, so size = s. Restore the bytes. No wrap up to 8 MB means 16 MB. Also verify a magic header and block checksums after loading: a missing or stale REU returns valid-looking stale data without error.
- **`$FF00` trigger** (b4 = 0): set the command, change `$01` (e.g. to `$34` for RAM under I/O), then store to `$FF00`. Whether this reaches RAM under I/O on the C64U is unverified; the safe route is DMA into a normal-RAM bounce buffer then CPU copy. DMA writes to colour RAM (`$D800`) need I/O visible.
- Turbo: starting a transfer must halt the CPU in the same cycle as the `$DF01` write. Firmware before 2026-08-28 could run instructions after the command write while DMA was in flight on U64-class cores. Put no instruction after `sta $DF01` that depends on the transfer or on stable REU registers, add `nop nop`, and disable interrupts from first register write to the trigger.

records.text:

# Ultimate Command Interface (UCI)

**Summary:** UCI is a polled register interface at `$DF1B-$DF1F` through which a C64 program asks the Ultimate to read/write files, open sockets, make HTTP requests, load files straight into RAM or REU, change the palette and reboot. It is off by default. Commands are `<target> <command> <args>`; replies are data bytes plus a status string. Targets: 1/2 DOS, 3 Network, 4 Control, 5 SoftwareIEC, 6 HTTP.
**Read when:** a game must load levels or data from the Ultimate's storage, save high scores, change the palette, use the network, or detect an Ultimate.

Marks: "(unverified)" = inferred. Dates = when added to public firmware master (github.com/GideonZ/1541ultimate); a device may be older. No UCI version command exists: try the command, check for `21,UNKNOWN COMMAND`. Docs: https://1541u-documentation.readthedocs.io/en/latest/uci/index.html. SDK (MIT): https://github.com/chrisgleissner/ultimate-uci-sdk. Enable with `c64_config` ("C64 and Cartridge Settings" / `Command Interface` = Enabled).

records.name: data/ultimate/uci.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/uci.md#Target 4: Control -->
**Palette `$51-$54`** (U64-class only; U2 answers `21`; firmware 2026-09-03 on; wrong length gives `81`): 8 bits per channel, takes effect on the whole display at once, live only (reset restores defaults; nothing saved). Whole palette costs about a quarter of a frame at 1 MHz, one colour about an eighth; per-frame changes are fine, per-raster-line are not. A blocking write can take 12-58 ms (measured on a C64U), so in a time-critical display issue it as a non-blocking step per frame (push command, poll status once per frame, finish later, one command in flight) or under a fade. Send `04 54` on exit. Raw: `04 53 02 FF FF FF` colour 2 to white. See also c64://ultimate/upic.

**LOAD_CONFIG** (`04 50 <name>`, default `/temp/uci_config.cfg`): the only config entry point. Write a `.cfg` via DOS, then send. Format: `[Store Name]` then `Item=value` lines; `#`/`;` comments; only listed items change; unknown stores skipped; stores are applied immediately. Stores: `[C64 and Cartridge Settings]` (`Command Interface`, REU items), `[U64 Specific Settings]` (`Turbo Control`, `CPU Speed`, `Badline Timing`, `System Mode`, `Palette Definition`, video items), `[Audio Mixer]` (`Vol ...`, `Pan ...`), SID address items. Value strings must match the menu exactly; use a `.cfg` saved from the menu as template. Flash persistence is unverified (assume session only). The reply holds a parse log on errors.

# Upic: 384x256 16-Colour Graphics by Border Racing

**Summary:** Upic is a software technique by Aleksi Eeben, not a hardware mode and not a register. With the VIC display disabled (`$D011` bit 4 = 0) the whole screen is border, and the CPU, running at Ultimate turbo speed, stores a colour to `$D020` once per pixel, cycle-exact against the raster beam. Result: 384x256, 16 colours (from the runtime palette), no colour clash, no hardware sprites, no text. It needs an Ultimate 64 / Elite / Elite II / C64U at top turbo speed, PAL. Game code gets roughly 17-27% of each frame.
**Read when:** a request mentions Upic, a full-screen 16-colour bitmap without attribute clash on an Ultimate, or a game that scrolls and animates by palette cycling.

Marks: "(unverified)" = inferred or untested. Credit: Upic by Aleksi Eeben (https://csdb.dk/release/?id=263889). Public implementations: https://github.com/chrisgleissner/mandelbrot-upic (Xander Mol, Christian Gleissner; Oscar64) and https://github.com/xahmol/ultimate-uci-oscar64 (library with Upic renderer, GPL-3: read for reference, do not paste its code into other-licensed projects). Cross-references: c64://ultimate/hardware (turbo), c64://ultimate/uci (palette commands), c64://ultimate/reu (REU data), c64://graphics/vic/spec.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/upic.md#Requirements -->
## Requirements

| Need | Detail |
|---|---|
| Machine | Ultimate 64, Elite (48 MHz), Elite II, C64U (64 MHz). Not U2 cartridges, not a stock C64, not VICE (logic and buffers can be tested in VICE; the picture cannot). |
| Video | PAL only (NTSC untested) |
| Turbo | Turbo Control set to the registers value (`U64 Turbo Registers`, or `C64U Turbo Registers` on C64U), CPU Speed at top entry; program then writes `$D031` = `$8F` (index 15, badlines suppressed). Set with `c64_config` or a `.cfg` named like the PRG (same folder, run from the Ultimate file browser). A `.cfg` may list both Turbo Control lines; each firmware skips the value it does not know (unverified). |
| UCI | `Command Interface` = Enabled, for palette commands (c64://ultimate/uci) |
| Firmware | palette commands: 3.15 or later on U64 family (development builds after 3.15); C64U needs a firmware that has them (shipped by 1.2.1 on one measured C64U) |

- Index 15 gives 48 MHz or 64 MHz depending on model; the register cannot tell. Probe (c64://ultimate/hardware).
- After any reset or program start the CPU runs at 1 MHz for about 2 s whatever `$D031` says. Wait it out (probe until two loop results agree) before the first frame.

records.name: data/ultimate/upic.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/upic.md#Renderer and CPU budget -->
## Renderer and CPU budget

- Per picture line: wait for the raster line, resync turbo by writing `$D031` = `$80` then `$8F` (so the CPU resumes at the same sub-slot on every line), then call a generated, page-aligned routine: patch-list loads, a delay loop, then per byte column: load byte, store to `$D020` (low nybble), table lookup `nyb[i] = i >> 4`, store to `$D020` (high nybble). End with two NOPs (without them pixel 383 is lost) and `$D020` = 0.
- 64 MHz: 63 CPU cycles per phi2 (VIC takes one of 64 sub-slots), 3,969 per PAL line; two pixels per 16 cycles, 16 pixels in 126 cycles; all 384 pixels one dot wide.
- 48 MHz: 47 cycles per phi2, 2,961 per line; 3 of every 4 pixels are shown (288 effective), some pixels 2 dots wide or off by one dot; free CPU time about three quarters of 64 MHz (measured ratio 0.75: 2,961 against 3,969 cycles per PAL line blanked, 2026-11-13).
- Never use indexed stores to I/O in the renderer (extra dummy read changes timing); a VIC register read costs one extra sub-slot, a write none.
- Renderer takes about 82% of a frame at 256 rows. Free CPU cycles per 64 MHz frame, measured on a C64U (50 samples, with a status marker row on):

| Visible rows | Free cycles / frame |
|---|---|
| 256 | about 204,800 |
| 240 | about 268,300 |
| 224 | about 331,000 |

- Frame rate is the display refresh (50 Hz) as long as per-frame work fits the free time. If it overruns, raster lines shift and rows glitch; polled loops that call "show frame" between work chunks show the picture only on some frames (flicker). Interrupt-driven display (raster IRQ at about line `$17`, hook at end of frame) keeps it steady.
- Showing fewer rows (a window) gives that time back at about 1/312 of a frame per row.
- Measured per-frame costs of a ring-buffer scroller (cycle model, 64 MHz): horizontal one new column about 3.8k cycles (left 4.2k), vertical one new row about 51k, diagonal about 53k.
- Naive full-screen clear/fill (49,152 byte stores at 4-5 cycles each) takes about a full frame of free time (derived, unverified): do not clear the screen per frame.

records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/upic.md#What is impossible -->
## What is impossible

- Hardware sprites (invisible while DEN = 0, tested on hardware), text mode, bitmap/multicolour modes, colour RAM, raster bars by IRQ, any second raster interrupt, stable KERNAL IRQ chain. Anything that moves must be drawn into the buffer by software.
- Per-line palette tricks (UCI is far too slow). VICE preview of the picture.
- Interrupts and stalls inside the picture: CIA timer IRQs must be off; KERNAL/BASIC IRQ handlers must be bypassed (own vectors with ROMs out, `$01 = $35`; NMI to an RTI). **Host-side REST access (`c64_memory` read, screen capture) stalls the CPU** through DMA: in a measurement, 29 REST reads over 1500 frames produced 19 glitched frames, none without. Avoid it while Upic runs.

records.name: data/ultimate/upic.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/upic.md#Detection and fallback -->
## Detection and fallback

- Run all checks on the normal text screen BEFORE setting DEN = 0 and print a plain message naming the setting to change: Command Interface off (`$DF1D & $7F != $49`), turbo registers missing (`$D031 = $FF`; `$00` suggests TurboEnable Bit mode, check `$D030`), speed not 64 MHz (a 48 MHz machine gets a degraded picture), palette commands missing (try GET_PALETTE `04 51`, retry about 10 times 0.2 s apart right after boot; error 21 means old firmware or a U2), REU too small (size probe in c64://ultimate/reu).
- Speed probe and model: c64://ultimate/hardware. The product string cannot tell a C64U from an original U64.
- No graphical fallback exists in the libraries: without turbo the renderer produces garbage. Offer a normal VIC mode path or refuse to start.
- Exit recipe is undocumented (unverified): stop the raster IRQ, set DEN = 1 in `$D011`, `$D031` = 0, restore `$01`, vectors, `$D020`, and send `04 54` to reset the palette.

records.name: data/ultimate/upic.md
records.text:
<!-- Source: data/ultimate/upic.md#Pitfalls -->
## Pitfalls

1. Upic is a technique: do not generate code expecting a mode register or a second VIC.
2. Wait out the 1 MHz window; a PRG started without its turbo `.cfg` never reaches speed (probe gives up).
3. No indexed addressing on I/O, no interrupts or DMA stalls mid-frame, no REST memory reads.
4. UCI discipline: write literal control values, bound all loops, do not send the unlock sequence if UCI already answers.
5. Compiler pitfalls with Oscar64 seen in these projects: reordered constant I/O stores (use inline asm for DMA), dropped reads of `$DC0D` (do it in asm), globals shared with the IRQ must be volatile, a data region below `$0801` moves the PRG load address.
6. `.upic` file saving needs a real UCI directory; after reset the current directory can be virtual and creation fails.
7. Display of 240 rows instead of 256 buys about 30% more free time.

### Task ID Convention

Each task folder name equals its **`task.id`**, constructed as:

```text
<4-digit counter>_<task.name>
```

Example:

```text
0001_extract_sprites
0002_extract_sprites
0003_extract_ram
```

Counters increment per new task creation (shared across both task types).  
All background tasks are placed under `tasks/background/`, all foreground tasks under `tasks/`.
